Brachial plexus injury

In one small randomized trial after Oberlin nerve transfer, more PBM-treated patients showed reinnervation and mean muscle power was higher at three months. The result needs independent confirmation.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one small randomized trial after Oberlin nerve transfer, more PBM-treated patients showed reinnervation and mean muscle power was higher at three months. The result needs independent confirmation.

Summary of the Evidence

One exact-category publication reports a prospective randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 14 patients with brachial plexus injury after Oberlin neurotization, a nerve-transfer operation. Seven patients received PBM and seven received placebo treatment. No duplicate report or independent second trial was identified. The findings therefore apply to this postoperative setting and should not be treated as evidence for all brachial plexus injuries.

Human and clinical evidence

At three months, a greater number of patients in the PBM group showed signs of reinnervation, and mean muscle power was significantly higher than in the control group. The study followed participants for six months and reported no treatment-related adverse effects. These findings indicate an early difference in nerve and motor recovery in the tested group. The publication does not provide replicated estimates from a larger sample, so the size and durability of the advantage remain uncertain (Foo et al. 2020).

Animal evidence

No animal experiment directly examining PBM after brachial plexus injury was identified in this indication category. Studies of other peripheral nerves or injury models would be indirect evidence and are not counted here.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly tied to this clinical indication was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used continuous 808-nm near-infrared light at 50 mW and 4 J/cm². Treatment was given daily for ten treatment days after nerve transfer, with clinical follow-up to six months. The database does not identify a head-to-head comparison of wavelengths, doses, or treatment schedules. Because every participant underwent the same type of operation, the result does not establish effects in untreated injuries, other nerve-transfer procedures, or longstanding paralysis.

Interpretation

The randomized trial found higher mean muscle power and more observed reinnervation in the PBM group at three months. These are relevant recovery outcomes, not merely laboratory markers. The trial is too small to give a stable estimate, however, and a separate group has not yet confirmed the result.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for early reinnervation and muscle-strength improvement after Oberlin neurotization
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One sham-controlled randomized trial found more reinnervation and higher mean muscle power after PBM in patients who had undergone Oberlin nerve transfer. The direction of these clinical outcomes supports further testing, but only 14 people took part. A larger independent trial with blinded strength and nerve-conduction measures, consistent surgery, and longer follow-up would show whether the early differences are reliable and lasting.
